conventions.convention: Scores are relative to a specified differentiable family of finite-valued measurable density representatives selected under AC. No parameter measurability or common exceptional null set follows from domination alone. The score is zero where the density is zero.
Scalar information is the possibly infinite expected squared score. Vector information is the second-moment matrix of a square-integrable score; equality with its covariance requires mean zero.

The information-identity theorem uses fixed positive support outside one common null set, continuous first and second parameter partial derivatives, integrable uniform derivative envelopes, and a finite score second moment. These are sufficient conditions, not necessary conditions for valid score identities.

The scalar bound assumes the estimator's mean equals the target locally, a finite second moment at the chosen parameter, mean-zero score, finite strictly positive information, and the covariance-derivative identity. Equality is a pointwise-parameter almost-sure assertion, including when the target derivative is zero.

The vector bound uses a k-by-d target Jacobian, nonsingular d-by-d information, pointwise estimator mean and second moments, and an explicitly assumed k-by-d score-derivative identity. Matrix order means nonnegativity of every quadratic form.

load_bearing.statement: On positive density, the score is the parameter gradient of the log density, extended by zero on zero density. Scalar Fisher information is Eθ[Sθ²]; for a square-integrable vector score, its information matrix is Eθ[SθSθᵀ]. These definitions are relative to the specified differentiable representative family.

Assume AC, an open parameter domain, a fixed sigma-finite dominator, locally fixed positive support outside one common null set, continuous first and second density partial derivatives with integrable uniform envelopes, and a finite score second moment at θ. Then EθSθ=0 and, entrywise, I(θ)=Eθ[SθSθᵀ]=−Eθ[∇²ℓθ].

Assume AC. On an open scalar parameter interval, fix θ and a target ψ differentiable at θ. If a real estimator T has EηT=ψ(η) locally, EθT²<∞, the score has mean zero and I(θ)∈(0,∞), and Covθ(T,Sθ)=ψ′(θ), then Varθ(T)≥ψ′(θ)²/I(θ). Equality holds exactly when T−ψ(θ)=(ψ′(θ)/I(θ))Sθ almost surely under Pθ.

Assume AC. At θ in an open subset of Rᵈ, let a measurable Rᵏ-valued estimator T have finite second moments and mean ψ(θ), where ψ is differentiable at θ. If the square-integrable score has mean zero, nonsingular information I(θ), and Eθ[(T−ψ(θ))Sθᵀ]=Dψ(θ), then Covθ(T)⪰Dψ(θ)I(θ)⁻¹Dψ(θ)ᵀ.

seams_checked.note: The opened domination and likelihood-density definitions supply a fixed sigma-finite dominator and AC-selected finite nonnegative density representatives. The score definition preserves their version dependence and lack of automatic parameter measurability or a common null set, adding differentiability explicitly.

The opened unbiasedness definition requires integrability and the correct mean at every parameter; finite-variance unbiasedness additionally requires global second moments. Both bounds correctly explain that this global class supplies their weaker local or pointwise mean-and-moment premises, while score-derivative identities remain separate.

The opened statistics definition imports the pointwise log-density score convention and explicitly assumes agreement with the QMD score at the true parameter. The opened QMD definition and mean-zero lemma provide a separate L² route; they do not claim pointwise differentiability follows from QMD.

The opened efficient-score definition identifies differentiable parametric scores with the supplier's coordinate log-density scores, separately assumes membership in L²₀, and defines efficient information as a second-moment matrix. It does not infer mean zero or nonsingularity from the score definition.
